title: Make an advocate (Avot 4:11)
hook: a reference call you'll never hear: each good deed gains an advocate, each wrong an accuser
tomorrow: the cast is fighting. which meetings actually last?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Meir: lessen your business, busy yourself with Torah, be humble before every person. Less business. Today, a courtroom.

Somewhere right now, a phone rings, and a manager asks about a person who isn't on the line. What's she like? Would you hire her again? The person never hears the answer. Who speaks up for you in a room you're not in? Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says you already know. You've been hiring them, one at a time, with your own hands.
screen: `A CALL YOU'LL NEVER HEAR.` → `WHO SPEAKS FOR YOU?` → `YOU HIRED THEM YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's his saying, in plain words. Whoever does one mitzvah, one commandment, gains one advocate. Whoever commits one wrong gains one accuser. And return and good deeds, he adds, are like a shield. Listen to the words he picks. The Hebrew for advocate is praklit: a defender who stands up in court and speaks for you. The accuser is kateigor: the one who stands on the other side and names what you did. The picture is a courtroom, and your own deeds are the speakers. Not a scoreboard. A voice. Each good act becomes someone on your side of the room. Each wrong becomes someone on the other side. And the shield matters, because the saying doesn't leave you stuck with your accusers. Teshuvah, return, turning back from a wrong, stands up too. Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: in this saying, you don't just do a good deed. You gain a defender, one deed at a time, who speaks when you can't. That changes the size of a small act. Holding a door, returning what you borrowed, staying late to help: each one is a voice in a room you'll never see. Make an advocate.
screen: `ONE MITZVAH, ONE ADVOCATE.` · `ONE WRONG, ONE ACCUSER.` · `A VOICE, NOT A SCOREBOARD.` · `RETURN IS A SHIELD.` · then, large: `MAKE AN ADVOCATE.`

segments.voice: Rest both hands open on your knees, palms up. Let the right hand hold one good thing you did this week, however small, and feel its weight there as someone on your side. Let the left hand hold one thing you'd take back, and for the rest of the sit, slowly close the left hand, the way return closes the case.
screen: `HANDS OPEN, PALMS UP.` · `RIGHT: AN ADVOCATE.` · `LEFT: SLOWLY CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Make an advocate. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: each mitzvah gains a defender, each wrong an accuser, and return is a shield.
Your line: make an advocate, one small deed at a time. Thirty-three of sixty, and counting.

howItsDone: In Jewish teaching on the High Holy Days, teshuvah (return), prayer and charity are spoken of as what turns a hard decree aside, and many Jews take on small extra mitzvot in the weeks before Rosh Hashanah.

fork.setup: a new kid in your class keeps getting left out. helping him won't change your grade, and nobody's watching. in Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's picture, what does sitting with him at lunch do?
options: it gains you an advocate: a voice on your side in a room you'll never see.
nothing much, since only big public acts count in the courtroom.
it cancels out exactly one wrong, like subtracting points.
fork.reveal: each mitzvah, however small, gains one advocate. the courtroom isn't arithmetic, and it doesn't need witnesses.

original.note: Hebrew in the Mishnah: an advocate, a defender who speaks for you in court.

trapdoor: what you thought: do good, get points.
what it means: each good deed becomes a defender and each wrong an accuser, and return is a shield between you and the charge.
what a scholar hears: praklit and kateigor are courtroom words used in the Mishnah's Hebrew, and the saying pairs them with teshuvah as the defense.
